scope.note: Exactly 22 frozen model labels: 17 tomato/potato/corn/rice disease-or-healthy labels + 5 pest labels. Rice has no Healthy class in the frozen list.

important_constraint: This KB contains only the frozen 4-crop/22-class model scope. It does not contain prevention entries for any other crop.

model_class_verification.reason: The frozen labels supplied by the team are used here, but the actual PlantVillage/IP102/rice-dataset folder names were not available in this conversation. Do not rename model classes until the actual folders are inspected.
required_before_training: List actual rice-disease dataset folder names.
Resolve aliases such as Yellow leaf curl virus vs Tomato leaf curl virus only in a mapping layer.
Do not assign scientific pest names until the actual IP102 folder identity is verified.

display_policy.purpose: Compact side-feature prevention guidance after prediction.
display_policy.preferred_display: 3-5 concise prevention bullets, with optional 'Local tip' line.

prevention: Start with healthy seedlings and clean planting material.
Remove and destroy infected leaves and crop debris promptly.
Maintain adequate plant spacing and airflow; avoid prolonged leaf wetness.
Avoid overhead irrigation where practical and keep foliage as dry as possible.
Rotate tomato with non-host crops rather than repeatedly planting tomato in the same bed.
local_prevention: Prioritize sanitation and canopy drying during humid South-Indian weather.

prevention: Use healthy planting material and avoid introducing infected transplants.
Remove infected plant material promptly and destroy crop residues after harvest.
Maintain spacing and airflow to reduce prolonged leaf wetness.
Avoid unnecessary overhead irrigation and improve drainage.
Monitor closely during cool, wet and highly humid periods.
local_prevention: In humid monsoon conditions, drainage and rapid drying of foliage are particularly important.

prevention: Reduce humidity around foliage through adequate spacing, pruning and good airflow.
Avoid overhead watering and reduce prolonged leaf wetness.
Remove and destroy infected leaves and fallen debris.
Sanitize stakes, tools and protected-cultivation structures where relevant.
Use resistant varieties when available and appropriate.
local_prevention: Especially relevant to protected/high-humidity cultivation.

prevention: Remove and destroy infected leaves and crop debris.
Use adequate spacing and pruning to improve air circulation.
Water at the base rather than wetting foliage.
Use mulch to reduce soil splash onto lower leaves.
Rotate away from tomato and manage solanaceous weeds where practical.
local_prevention: TNAU specifically lists removal/destruction of affected plant parts and clean seed treatment as management measures.

prevention: Use clean, disease-free seed and healthy transplants.
Remove and destroy infected plant material and crop debris.
Avoid working through wet foliage because bacterial spread is favored by water.
Avoid overhead irrigation and reduce leaf wetness.
Maintain spacing and airflow and control volunteer plants/weeds.
local_prevention: Use sanitation and water-management measures first; avoid spreading contaminated material between plants.

prevention: Use virus-free, healthy transplants and resistant/tolerant varieties where available.
Control whitefly populations and reduce nearby weed/host reservoirs.
Remove severely infected plants when incidence is low enough for roguing to be useful.
Remove old tomato crop residues and volunteers promptly after harvest.
Avoid establishing new tomato plantings immediately beside heavily infected older crops.
local_prevention: The disease is virus-associated; prevention focuses on healthy planting material, whitefly management and sanitation rather than curing infected plants.

prevention: Continue using healthy planting material and clean tools.
Maintain balanced nutrition, adequate spacing and good drainage.
Avoid prolonged leaf wetness and unnecessary plant stress.
Scout plants regularly so early disease symptoms can be addressed promptly.
local_prevention: No disease-specific intervention is required for a healthy prediction.

prevention: Use healthy seed tubers and maintain good field sanitation.
Remove or manage infected crop residues after harvest.
Maintain balanced plant nutrition and avoid prolonged plant stress.
Use adequate spacing and irrigation practices that minimize extended leaf wetness.
Rotate crops where practical rather than continuous potato cultivation.
local_prevention: Prefer cultural and sanitation measures before any chemical intervention.

prevention: Plant healthy, disease-free seed tubers.
Avoid leaving infected volunteer potatoes or cull piles near the field.
Maintain good field drainage and avoid prolonged leaf wetness.
Remove infected foliage/residue appropriately to reduce inoculum.
During cool, wet weather, increase field scouting and act early on confirmed disease.
local_prevention: Late blight risk rises under cool, wet conditions; field sanitation and healthy seed are foundational.

prevention: Use certified/healthy seed tubers.
Maintain drainage, balanced nutrition and appropriate spacing.
Rotate crops where practical and remove volunteer/cull potatoes.
Scout regularly for early disease and pest signs.
Use hybrids with suitable resistance/tolerance where available.
Rotate away from continuous corn where practical.
Manage infected residue to reduce the local inoculum source.
Avoid unnecessarily dense canopies and prolonged leaf wetness.
Increase scouting under warm, humid conditions.
local_prevention: Humid South-Indian conditions can favor foliar disease development; prioritize canopy drying and residue management.

prevention: Use resistant/tolerant hybrids where available.
Maintain adequate spacing and airflow.
Avoid excessive canopy humidity and prolonged leaf wetness.
Scout regularly during favorable humid conditions.
Maintain balanced crop nutrition and avoid unnecessary plant stress.
local_prevention: General integrated foliar-disease prevention; do not infer a chemical treatment from the class alone.

prevention: Use hybrids with resistance/tolerance where available.
Rotate away from continuous corn where practical.
Reduce or properly manage infected corn residue.
Maintain adequate field airflow and avoid prolonged leaf wetness.
Scout early when humid/wet conditions persist.
local_prevention: Resistance plus cultural practices are the main preventive foundation.

prevention: Use healthy seed and suitable resistant/tolerant hybrids.
Maintain balanced nutrition, drainage and appropriate plant density.
Manage crop residue and avoid continuous corn where practical.
Scout regularly for foliar disease and insect damage.
Use healthy seed and resistant/tolerant varieties where recommended.
Avoid excessive nitrogen application and maintain balanced nutrition.
Manage field water carefully and avoid prolonged unnecessary standing water when disease is developing.
Maintain clean field sanitation and remove heavily infected material where practical.
Use integrated disease-management guidance from the local agriculture department.
local_prevention: Drainage/water management is particularly important when bacterial blight is developing.

prevention: Use healthy, quality seed and avoid carrying infected seed into the next crop.
Maintain balanced plant nutrition, especially avoiding nutrient stress.
Manage water so the crop does not undergo prolonged moisture stress.
Remove or properly manage infected crop residues and volunteer rice.
Use locally recommended tolerant/resistant varieties where available.
local_prevention: Brown spot can be associated with nutrient and water stress; maintaining crop vigor is a key preventive measure.

prevention: Use healthy, clean seed and avoid planting visibly infected seed lots.
Maintain balanced nutrition and avoid excessive nitrogen.
Remove/manage infected residues after harvest.
Use suitable tolerant/resistant varieties when locally recommended.
Maintain good field sanitation and avoid carrying infected material between fields.
local_prevention: The provided official rice IPM material supports integrated sanitation, healthy seed and balanced crop management; no unsupported chemical prescription is included.

prevention: Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization and very dense planting.
Use balanced fertilizer, especially split nitrogen applications.
Maintain appropriate field water management; drainage/alternate wetting and drying can reduce outbreak conditions.
Prefer resistant/tolerant varieties where available.
Use synchronized planting and avoid unnecessary continuous rice cultivation.
local_prevention: Do not recommend routine broad-spectrum spraying; preserve natural enemies and use threshold-based IPM.

prevention: Use synchronized planting where practical.
Avoid very close planting and prolonged water stagnation.
Use locally recommended resistant/tolerant varieties where available.
Remove/destroy egg masses and heavily infested plant parts when feasible.
Use pheromone traps and biological control as part of an IPM programme.
local_prevention: The label is preserved exactly as supplied by the model plan; the source used for prevention is the Indian rice yellow stem-borer/Scirpophaga incertulas guidance.

prevention: Avoid excessive nitrogen and overly dense crop canopies.
Conserve natural enemies and avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticide use.
Monitor leaf-folding damage regularly and use threshold-based IPM.
Use biological-control options such as parasitoids where locally recommended.
Maintain field sanitation and synchronized crop management where practical.
local_prevention: The class label is preserved exactly; prevention follows rice leaf-folder IPM guidance.

prevention: Use locally recommended resistant/tolerant hybrids where available.
Destroy or properly manage crop residues after harvest to reduce carry-over.
Scout early for egg masses and larval damage.
Maintain field sanitation and avoid leaving heavily infested residues.
Use pheromone/monitoring tools and biological control where available.
local_prevention: The exact IP102 class identity should be verified against the actual dataset folder before adding a species-specific scientific name.

prevention: Scout maize early and frequently for larvae and fresh feeding damage.
Remove and destroy visible larval infestations where practical.
Maintain field sanitation and manage weeds that can provide shelter/host sites.
Use biological and botanical IPM options where locally recommended.
Avoid unnecessary insecticide use so natural enemies are conserved.
local_prevention: This prevention entry is intentionally IPM-focused and does not prescribe a chemical dose. The exact IP102 label should be verified before assigning a scientific name.
